clue.text: Stupid character bunglin' heists now and again

parts.note: bungling is fluffing; the dropped g of the clue's slangy spelling drops it from the synonym too

indicators.note: taking letters only now and again means every other letter of heists, starting with the second

parts.note: its second, fourth and sixth letters are the ones taken

explanation.surface: A dim-witted crook keeps messing up robberies, every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in bunglin' is doing work: it tells you the synonym also loses its final G.
explanation.definitionFit: Fluffiness as a personality trait is airheaded silliness, a lightweight, dim quality of mind.

clue.text: Ersatz brass making Charlie a thousand

indicators.note: making Charlie into something else tells you to change that letter for the new one

parts.note: brass in the sense of cheek or nerve is face, as in 'to have the face to do it'
K, short for kilo, is the usual shorthand for a thousand, as in a salary of 50K

explanation.surface: Fake brass ornaments turn a bloke called Charlie into a thousandaire.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet; K is the usual shorthand for a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz describes an inferior imitation or substitute, so it is a synonym of counterfeit or bogus.

clue.text: Empty posh port around centre of Henley

indicators.note: the posh port goes around the other letters, holding them between its two parts

parts.note: U is the old label for upper-class usage, hence posh
Aden is the port city in Yemen

indicators.note: centre of picks out the middle letters of the six-letter word

parts.note: the centre of six-letter Henley is its two middle letters

explanation.surface: A smart riverside town sits empty around the Henley regatta.
explanation.definitionFit: Unladen means carrying no load or cargo, so a ship or lorry described that way is empty.

clue.text: Maybe nineteenth hole lacking in cocktail? A little

parts.note: one nineteenth is an example of a fraction, signalled by Maybe

indicators.note: lacking in says the drink is missing that letter somewhere inside

parts.note: an alloy is a mixture of metals, a metallurgical cocktail
O is a hole by its shape

explanation.surface: A golfer at the nineteenth hole, the clubhouse bar, finds their cocktail a little short.
explanation.walkthrough: The nineteenth hole is golf slang for the clubhouse bar, which steers you to drinks; here it splits into a number and an O.
explanation.definitionFit: Fractionally is an adverb meaning by a very small amount, slightly.

clue.text: OK to take new unit reduced to eleven hundred?

definitions.note: OK to take, the adjective safe to swallow; to take is linking

indicators.note: reduced trims the last letter from the word for unit

parts.note: one is the unit number
taken as written
XI is eleven in Roman numerals, and also a cricket or football side
C is a hundred in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Is it all right to take on a new unit cut back to eleven hundred people?
explanation.definitionFit: Something non-toxic is harmless, safe to eat or handle, so it is fine or acceptable.

clue.text: When heavenward, having unending belief?

indicators.note: heavenward, in a down clue, means read upwards, so the word turns round

parts.note: as in the sense of when, as in 'as he arrived'

indicators.note: unending removes the final letter

parts.note: a credo is a statement of belief

explanation.surface: One looking up to heaven, holding a faith without limit.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a picture of holiness: something gazing heavenward with endless faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacred means holy, connected with religion and the divine, the realm of belief and heaven.

clue.text: Scouse, for one in Devon area, extremely troublesome

indicators.note: in places the outer letters inside the regional abbreviation

parts.note: Devon is in the south-west of England, SW

indicators.note: extremely means taking the extremes, the first and last letters

parts.note: its first and last letters are wanted

explanation.surface: A Liverpudlian visiting Devon proves extremely troublesome.
explanation.walkthrough: Scouse is a Liverpool lamb or beef stew (and gives Liverpudlians their nickname); the surface wants the person.
explanation.definitionFit: Scouse is a meat and vegetable stew from Liverpool, so it is one example of that dish.

clue.text: The unknown's all right, apparently

parts.note: taken as written
y is an algebraic unknown, and the 's adds S
ay is an old form of yes, agreeing that all is right

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs that the unknown is fine, or so it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: They say introduces hearsay, what is reportedly true, so it works like seemingly or reportedly.

clue.text: Possibly deal with money bypassing the works director

parts.note: deal is a kind of pine or fir timber, so possibly deal is wood

indicators.note: the money goes around everything, its letters passing either side

parts.note: the yen is the Japanese currency
the works is everything, all

explanation.surface: Perhaps a deal with cash goes ahead, skipping the factory's director.
explanation.walkthrough: Deal looks like a business agreement but is the softwood; the director is the American film-maker of Annie Hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Woody Allen is a famous American film-maker, so he is an example of a movie director.

clue.text: Boot bags normal when shifting football outfit

indicators.note: bags in the sense of grabs and holds, so the kick encloses the rest

parts.note: to boot a ball is to kick it

indicators.note: shifting tells you the letters of normal move into a new order

explanation.surface: A footballer's kit bag holds his usual boots as the team changes.
explanation.walkthrough: Kilmarnock is a Scottish professional football club from Ayrshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Kilmarnock FC is a Scottish club, and outfit is an informal word for a team or organisation.

clue.text: Lake I built without spending much

definitions.note: an adjectival sense: a Lego building is a flimsy, cheap-looking toy-brick construction

parts.note: the ego is the self, the I

explanation.surface: On the lake I put up a cheap little structure.
explanation.walkthrough: Ego is Latin for I, and the self in psychology.
explanation.definitionFit: Critics call cheap modular architecture Lego, comparing such buildings to plastic toy bricks snapped together.

clue.text: Brother in comprehensive education that contests steeplechase?

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for one that races, a horse; the question mark marks it as an example

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for brother inside the other letters

parts.note: thorough means complete, comprehensive

explanation.surface: A brother at a comprehensive school asks about a steeplechase race.
explanation.walkthrough: Comprehensive hints at the British state secondary school, but here it simply means thorough.
explanation.definitionFit: A thoroughbred is a pedigree racehorse breed, the kind of animal that runs in steeplechases.

clue.text: Revise bright idea withdrawing clothes

indicators.note: withdrawing means going back, so the concealed word reads in reverse
clothes as a verb, covering, so the phrase dresses a word inside it

parts.note: the word sits across the join of the two words, brighT IDEa

explanation.surface: Change your inspired notion and stop taking clothes away.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit a text is to correct and amend it, which is what revising means.

clue.text: Dare-devil keeps gatecrashing public inquiry at back

indicators.note: gatecrashing means barging in uninvited, so these letters go inside

parts.note: overt means open, done in public
to keep something is to have it, so keeps gives has

indicators.note: at back means the last letter of inquiry

parts.note: its final letter is the one taken

explanation.surface: A reckless type keeps bursting into the open hearings of a public inquiry.
explanation.definitionFit: A dare-devil, used as an adjective, means reckless, and overhasty means rash, acting too quickly.

clue.text: Somewhere in mid-Europe, underwear model on the up — hot stuff!

parts.note: a bra is women's underwear

indicators.note: in a down entry, on the up means the word reads upwards, backwards

parts.note: to model for an artist is to sit
lava is molten rock, literally hot stuff

explanation.surface: A lingerie model is rising to fame somewhere in Central Europe; she's hot stuff.
explanation.definitionFit: Bratislava is the capital of Slovakia, a city in central Europe on the Danube.

clue.text: Ladder repositioned to short fire escape, hopefully

definitions.note: a verb phrase: to make a dash for it, hoping to get away

parts.note: a ladder in tights is a run

indicators.note: repositioned means the letters are moved into a different order
short means cut down by a final letter

explanation.surface: A ladder is moved up to a burning building as a fire escape.
explanation.walkthrough: Ladder and fire escape conjure a rescue, but the ladder is the kind you get in stockings.
explanation.definitionFit: To run for it is to flee suddenly, trying to get clear of danger or capture.

clue.text: Merchant ship avoiding huge lochs in this region?

indicators.note: avoiding means the ship leaves those letters out

parts.note: an argosy is a large merchant ship
OS is the clothing size outsize, so huge
L is the map abbreviation for loch, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Trading vessels keep clear of the big lakes in this part of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Argyll is a Scottish region of sea lochs, so the question mark points to lochs being in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Argyll is a historic county and area of western Scotland, famous for its lochs and coast.

clue.text: British audio broadcast features outwardly chic heroine

indicators.note: features means includes, so the reshuffled letters hold the others
broadcast means scattered about, so the letters of audio are mixed
outwardly means the outside letters, first and last

parts.note: its outer letters are wanted

explanation.surface: A British radio programme spotlights a stylish heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: Boudicca was queen of the Iceni, who led a revolt against Roman Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Boudicca is celebrated as a national heroine of ancient Britain for leading a rebellion against Rome.

clue.text: Slogger run out by Jack intercepting hit

indicators.note: intercepting means getting in the way, so these letters go inside

parts.note: to tan someone is to beat them, as in tanning their hide
RO is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out
J is the abbreviation for a jack in cards

explanation.surface: A big-hitting batsman is run out after a fielder named Jack cuts off his shot.
explanation.walkthrough: Slogger looks like a batsman, but here it means a hard worker: to work like a trojan.
explanation.definitionFit: A trojan is someone who works with great energy and endurance, a tireless toiler.

clue.text: How one casts old commandos, screening detective series?

indicators.note: screening means hiding behind, so the other letters wrap around

parts.note: RM is the Royal Marines, Britain's commandos
Vera is a British TV detective drama

explanation.surface: How a director casts old commandos while filming a detective show.
explanation.walkthrough: Casts suggests choosing actors; it is throwing, as in casting a ball or a line.
explanation.definitionFit: An overarm throw is made with the arm above the shoulder, a way of bowling or throwing.

clue.text: Flirt disheartened still visiting French coast

indicators.note: visiting means calling in, so the trimmed word goes inside

parts.note: côte is French for coast

indicators.note: disheartened means losing the heart, the central letter

parts.note: still means quiet, calm

explanation.surface: A dispirited flirt still pays visits to the French coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A coquette is a woman who teases or flirts, toying with admirers' affections.

clue.text: Note to split chopped dog food

indicators.note: to split means breaking into the word, so the letter sits inside
chopped means the tail is cut off

parts.note: a terrier is a breed of dog

explanation.surface: A memo asks for chopped-up dog food to be divided.
explanation.walkthrough: Dog food tempts as one unit; dog belongs to the wordplay and food alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrine is a coarse pâté-like dish cooked in an earthenware mould, so it is a type of dish.

clue.text: Perhaps monitor student magician removing head

parts.note: L for learner, the plate on a learner driver's car

indicators.note: removing head means taking off the first letter

parts.note: a wizard is a magician

explanation.surface: A student wizard is perhaps a class monitor once he loses his head.
explanation.walkthrough: Monitor suggests a screen or a prefect; it is the monitor lizard.
explanation.definitionFit: The monitor is a large reptile such as the Komodo dragon, one kind of lizard.

clue.text: Without issue, bill folded through last entrance

parts.note: SP is the legal abbreviation for sine prole, without children

indicators.note: through means passing inside, so the jumbled letters go in

parts.note: end, the last part

indicators.note: folded means bent out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A childless man's bill is folded up and slipped through the last door.
explanation.walkthrough: Entrance looks like a noun for a doorway; it is the verb, to enchant.
explanation.definitionFit: To spellbind someone is to hold them enthralled, as though under a spell, which is to entrance them.

clue.text: Motor locks resounded

definitions.note: the verb to motor, move fast

indicators.note: resounded means echoed, so the word is given by its sound

parts.note: locks are tresses of hair

explanation.surface: A car's lock mechanism clanked loudly.
explanation.definitionFit: To hare is to run very fast, like the animal, and to motor is to go quickly too.

clue.text: Close pocket when cycling

indicators.note: cycling moves a letter round from one end of the word to the other

parts.note: to pocket money is to take it in, earn it

explanation.surface: Shut your pocket while riding your bike.
explanation.definitionFit: Near means close at hand, a short distance away.

clue.text: Hallmark on label distinguished fruit

parts.note: AC, appellation contrôlée, is the quality mark printed on a French wine label
A1 means first-rate, and written as AI it looks like letters

explanation.surface: A quality stamp on the packaging marks out premium fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: AI stands for A1, top-class; AC is the French wine-label guarantee of origin.
explanation.definitionFit: Acai is a small purple Amazonian palm berry sold as a health food, so it is a fruit.

clue.text: Top sportsman reddish hosting constant workout

parts.note: a dan is a black-belt grade in judo and karate, a top martial artist

indicators.note: hosting means taking in a guest, so the colour holds the letter

parts.note: cerise is a cherry-red colour
c is the constant for the speed of light

explanation.surface: A star athlete flushed pink while putting on a steady workout.
explanation.definitionFit: Dancercise is an exercise regime based on dance moves, a kind of fitness session.

clue.text: American intermingled with railway crowd

indicators.note: intermingled means mixed together, so the two pieces are combined into a new order

explanation.surface: An American mingled with the throng at the station.
explanation.definitionFit: An army can mean a huge number of people, a multitude or horde.

clue.text: Artist's teddy bear ultimately charcoal rather than black

indicators.note: rather than says one letter takes the place of the other

parts.note: Edward Bear is the formal name of Winnie-the-Pooh, the most famous teddy bear

indicators.note: ultimately means the last letter of charcoal

parts.note: its final letter is the one taken

explanation.surface: An artist sketches a teddy bear, finishing in charcoal rather than black ink.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Lear, the nonsense poet, was also a landscape painter and illustrator.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear was a Victorian landscape painter and illustrator as well as a writer of limericks.
